messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar has worked the late shift at the same downtown burger joint for six years. At forty-one, he appreciated the quiet predictability of it: the rhythmic sizzle of the grill, the hum of the fluorescent lights after the dinner rush, the familiar faces of the city’s night owls. That predictability was shattered four months ago. It was close to midnight when two men came in, not for food, but for the register. One of them vaulted the counter while the other held a gun on the only customer, a young student waiting for her order. Omar froze behind the fry station. The man with the gun screamed at the student to get on the floor, his voice cracking with a vicious energy that filled the small space. When she hesitated, he shoved her hard, and her head hit the corner of a table with a sickening thud. The sound, sharp and final, has stayed with him. The assailant then turned on Omar, yelling at him to stop staring, to get the money, his words a barrage of criticism and threat that made Omar feel pinned to the spot, utterly helpless.

In the weeks that followed, the world outside his small apartment began to feel fundamentally unsafe. The primary driver of his distress, the engine of his fear, is the way ordinary moments now instantly signal extreme danger. This connection is immediate and absolute. A car backfiring on his street is no longer just a noise; for Omar, it is the sound of a gunshot, and he will drop to the floor, his heart hammering against his ribs, certain that the violence has found its way to his door. He is constantly scanning his environment, on high alert for any sudden or unexpected sound, believing that each one is a prelude to another attack. This intense monitoring has exhausted him, leaving him perpetually on edge.

This transformation of neutral cues into imminent threats is most acute at his job, the very place he once felt competent and secure. Last week, his manager, a woman he has known for years, pointed out that he had put the wrong sauce on a special order. Her tone was mild, but for Omar, being corrected felt identical to the robber’s aggressive screaming. In that instant, his manager’s face seemed to morph into the assailant’s, and a wave of terror washed over him. He was certain he was about to be hurt. He dropped the burger and backed away, unable to speak, leaving his manager confused and concerned. Any form of criticism, no matter how small or gently delivered, now triggers this profound conviction that he is in immediate physical danger.

As a result, Omar’s life has shrunk to the four walls of his apartment. He sees it as his only true safe zone. The journey to and from work is a gauntlet of potential threats. When the bus is even a minute late, he doesn’t feel impatient; he feels a rising panic, certain that the delay means something terrible has happened up the road and that he is trapped, exposed. The approach of midnight, the time the robbery occurred, brings a palpable sense of dread each day. As the clock ticks closer, he feels the walls of his apartment closing in, the only place he feels any semblance of safety. He finishes his shift and rushes home, locking and bolting the door behind him, his work uniform still on. He has stopped answering calls from his family and the few friends he has left. He came to therapy because his manager told him he needed to get help or risk losing his job. More than that, though, Omar is tired of being so afraid. He wants to be able to hear a loud noise without diving for cover, to take a bus without planning his escape, but he cannot shake the deep-seated belief that the moment he lets his guard down, the violence will happen all over again.
